title: Tight post-GST latency bounds for deterministic Byzantine agreement
open: Is it possible to pin down the exact latency of deterministic Byzantine agreement after global stabilization, rather than just its asymptotics? Formally, under eventual synchrony with n parties, t < n/3 Byzantine faults, and authenticated channels, close the gap between the classic t+1-round lower bound and the best post-GST upper bounds, determining the optimal leading constants and additive terms — with fault-dependent worst-case latency, good-case (correct-leader) latency, and voting phases within a successful view each stated separately, and views, communication rounds, and elapsed time treated as distinct metrics.
status: The t+1-round synchronous lower bound is classic (Dwork–Lynch–Stockmeyer, JACM 1988 — also the source of the eventual-synchrony model with GST and Δ). Linear-in-t post-GST time is achieved: Lewis-Pye (arXiv:2201.01107, Thm 1.3) gives O(tΔ) termination after GST with O(n²) communication, while SQuad (arXiv:2208.09262) treats linear worst-case fault-dependent latency as asymptotically optimal and separates consensus-within-view from view synchronisation. HotStuff (arXiv:1803.05069) established linear per-view communication and responsiveness but not a bound on faulty-leader view counts; HotStuff-2 (eprint 2023/397, Malkhi–Nayak) reduces within-view commit to two phases under responsiveness. Exact constants under matched assumptions remain open, and any gap claim requires fixing validity, setup, communication, and responsiveness constraints first.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower post-GST latency bounds are established under matched assumptions (validity, setup, communication, and responsiveness constraints fixed), with exact leading constants and additive terms separating fault-dependent worst-case latency from good-case (correct-leader) latency and accounting for voting phases within a successful view — improving on the current O(t·Δ) time / O(n²) communication upper bound of Lewis-Pye (2022) relative to the t+1-round lower bound.
why: Every production BFT chain's worst-case latency is governed by these terms; the asymptotic race is over and the constant race lacks a precise statement — pinning it is a real theory contribution.
key_works: Dwork–Lynch–Stockmeyer, JACM 1988 (https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Lynch/jacm88.pdf); Lewis-Pye, arXiv:2201.01107; SQuad, arXiv:2208.09262; Yin et al. HotStuff, arXiv:1803.05069; Malkhi–Nayak HotStuff-2, eprint 2023/397.
aliases: Byzantine agreement exact latency; post-GST round bounds

title: Asynchronous consensus with sublinear communication
open: Determine the communication complexity floor of asynchronous Byzantine agreement with adaptive adversaries and standard cryptography.
status: Asynchronous BA classically costs O(n²) messages; 2022-2024 lines (DAG-based, "Blazing BDLS", King–Saia-style) push toward Õ(n) expected communication with cryptographic help; exact asymptotics for adaptive adversaries remain open.
why: Bandwidth is the scaling wall for large-validator-set consensus.
key_works: King–Saia, "Byzantine agreement in polynomial expected time", 2013; DAG-Rider (Keidar et al., PODC 2021); Bullshark (SOSP 2022).

title: Optimal clock synchronization under Byzantine faults
open: How closely can clocks be synchronized in a network where a fraction of nodes may fail in arbitrary (Byzantine) ways and message delays are uncertain? Determine the tight achievable skew as a function of network delay uncertainty and fault fraction, closing the gap between the Lundelius–Lynch upper bounds and the known constructions.
status: The classic results of Lundelius–Lynch (JACM 1984) give the n/(n−f) upper bounds from 1984, with recent improvements obtained under weaker assumptions along the Attiya–Dolev–Welch lines; the exact achievable region remains open.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds on achievable skew as a function of network delay uncertainty and fault fraction are established, in particular closing the gap between the Lundelius–Lynch (n/(n−f)) upper bounds and the existing constructions.

title: Cross-shard atomic commit without two-phase lock madness
open: Can a cross-shard transaction commit in a single round of communication — no blocking two-phase commit — while remaining safe under shard failures and live under asynchrony, and matching the latency of the best single-shard commit within constant factors?
status: The classical baseline is 2PC/3PC; Spanner-class TrueTime commits (Corbett et al., OSDI 2012) and Gray–Lamport consensus commit lines shaped the modern landscape; Sui/Sequencer-style owned-object bypasses avoid cross-shard coordination for special cases; one-round cross-shard commit under partial synchrony remains open.
solved_when: A commit protocol exists that achieves one-round cross-shard commit, safety under shard failures, liveness under asynchrony, and single-shard-comparable latency within constant factors.
why: Sharded blockchains and distributed databases both hit this exact wall; solving it removes the latency and blocking penalties that currently make cross-shard transactions far costlier than single-shard ones.
key_works: Corbett et al., "Spanner", OSDI 2012; Gray–Lamport consensus commit lines.
